must_remember: All distances in spherical mirrors are measured from the pole (P) following the New Cartesian Sign Convention.
The relation between focal length ($f$) and radius of curvature ($R$) is given by $f = \frac{R}{2}$ for paraxial rays.
The mirror formula is expressed as $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$.
A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, and diminished image for any real position of an object.
Transverse linear magnification is given by $m = \frac{h_i}{h_o} = -\frac{v}{u}$.
Longitudinal magnification for a small object along the principal axis is $m_L = -m^2$.
The focal length of a spherical mirror remains unchanged when immersed in water.
Spherical aberration caused by marginal rays can be minimized by using parabolic mirrors or stop diaphragms.
Power of a spherical mirror is defined as $P = -\frac{1}{f}$, where $f$ is in meters.

glossary.meaning: The geometric center of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror.
The point on the principal axis where paraxial rays parallel to the axis converge or appear to diverge.
The distance between the pole and the principal focus of a spherical mirror.
The radius of the hollow sphere of which the mirror is a part.
Light rays that are close to the principal axis and make small angles with it.
Light rays falling at large heights from the principal axis, contributing to spherical aberration.
A defect where marginal rays do not converge at the principal focus, leading to a blurred image.
The ratio of the length of the image along the axis to the length of the object along the axis.
